about: The explainers' facts ledger. One entry per claim a page makes; a page cites an entry as [[fact:<id>]]. status: verified (a dated source), accepted (widely accepted in the field, no source cited), observed (EVBench's own first-hand experience, no published record), unverified (drafts only, marked). accepted and observed need a rationale. Rules: src/explainers/CLAUDE.md.

facts.claim: Current is power divided by voltage: 350 kW is about 875 A at 400 V and about 440 A at 800 V.

sources.title: P = V × I (arithmetic)

facts.claim: A split pack charges both halves in parallel, so the charger sees half the pack voltage and its power is capped at about charger current × half-pack voltage.

sources.title: Series/parallel arithmetic; the topology is stated by Audi (see audi-ppe-bank-charging)

facts.claim: While a split pack charges its halves in parallel, whatever runs from the pack during the charge sees half the pack's usual voltage, so it has to work at that voltage.

sources.title: Series/parallel arithmetic: two halves in parallel present half the series voltage

facts.claim: A booster (DC-DC or motor boost) draws from a lower-voltage charger at around 420–450 V, and at 450 V at most, not at a 500 V charger's full output.
facts.rationale: The owner's field experience (2026-09-29): 'definitely not 500V, 450V max'. It sits in tension with Lucid's release, which says the Gravity's boost charges 'with the highest voltage that a charging station is capable of outputting' (lucid-gravity-400v-method); both fit if what a booster can actually draw from a '500V' station is about 450 V. EVBench tests logging charger-side voltage on a booster car would make it rank B. The Split Pack Lab uses 450 V (BOOSTER_INPUT_V in peakOnCharger.js) and flags it on screen.

facts.claim: Resistive heat in the cells is I²R, so at the same pack voltage, charging at 225 kW makes about (225/400)² ≈ 32 % of the heat of charging at 400 kW.

sources.title: Joule heating, Q = I²R (arithmetic; assumes equal pack voltage and resistance)

facts.note: A model statement, not a measurement: it ignores the entropic term and the change of R with temperature and SoC.

facts.claim: At a charger's current limit, power scales with pack voltage: at 500 A, a pack at 288 V takes at most 144 kW, and one at 400 V 200 kW.

sources.title: P = V × I (arithmetic)

facts.claim: A Tesla V3 Supercharger post is rated 350 A continuous.

sources.title: r/teslamotors — 'V3 Supercharger live at Hawthorne, Los Angeles' (2019 photo of a V3 post)

facts.rationale: The owner has read the 350 A continuous rating on the post labels at many US V3 Supercharger sites. The 2019 Reddit photo is the only public record found; Reddit blocks automated reads, so Claude has not seen it. No Tesla document found.

facts.claim: Tesla V3 Superchargers boost above their 350 A continuous rating for a period, depending on conditions such as temperature and the equipment's own state: to about 500 A for non-Tesla vehicles, and well over 600 A for Tesla vehicles.
facts.rationale: Observed by EVBench and widely accepted (owner, 2026-09-28/29). A boost is by definition above the continuous rating for a limited time, and how long and how high depend on conditions. Charging logs (a run's kW against a known pack voltage) could make it rank B.

facts.claim: A Tesla V3 Supercharger cabinet delivers about 650 kW, shared across its 4 stalls.
facts.rationale: The owner's field knowledge (2026-09-28). No Tesla document found; the V4 Cabinet announcement says only that it powers 8 posts, '2X the stalls per cabinet'.

facts.claim: On a V3 cabinet, what limits one car's current is the post: a V4 post's higher-current cable and connector let the same cabinet deliver more current to one car than a V3 post can. That is how the Cybertruck reached 325 kW on V4 posts fed by V3 cabinets.
facts.rationale: The owner's explanation (2026-09-28): the cabinet's power is shared across stalls and was not the limit; the V3 post's cable was. Consistent with the post ratings: a V3 post is labeled 350 A continuous (tesla-v3-cable-current, observed) and a V4 post 615 A continuous (tesla-v4-post-ratings, verified).

facts.claim: A Tesla V4 Supercharger post is rated 500 kW for passenger vehicles, 615 A continuous, 0–1000 V DC.

sources.title: Tesla — Supercharger for Business, Technical Specifications

facts.claim: A Tesla V4 cabinet outputs 180–1000 V DC, up to 1200 kW shared by 8 posts.

sources.title: Tesla — Supercharger for Business, Technical Specifications

facts.claim: Tesla's V4 Cabinet (announced November 2024) supports 400–1000 V vehicles and delivers up to 500 kW for cars, with 30% faster charging for the Cybertruck; S3XY vehicles stay at the 250 kW they already get on a V3 Cabinet.

sources.title: @TeslaCharging on X, Nov 2024 — 'V4 Cabinet' announcement

facts.note: 250 kW is the S3XY vehicles' rate, not a cap on the V3 Cabinet, which the owner puts at about 650 kW shared across 4 stalls (tesla-v3-cabinet-shared). '30% faster for Cybertruck' matches 250 kW → 325 kW.

facts.claim: In the US, the DC fast chargers an 800 V-class pack cannot use directly are mainly older 50 kW units, which top out around 450–500 V, and Tesla Superchargers before V4, which top out at 500 V.

sources.title: Lucid Group press release, 28 Jan 2025: calls V3 Superchargers '500V architecture fast chargers' (a third party describing Tesla hardware)

facts.rationale: Accepted by the owner's decision (2026-09-28), from long field experience: it is the practical reason 400 V support matters in the US. Tesla's own page no longer lists a V3 cabinet voltage, and no other primary source was found. This is a product figure, which the accepted status normally excludes; the owner made an explicit exception.

facts.claim: The ABB Terra 360 (UL, CCS1) outputs 150–920 V DC, 350 A nominal and 500 A peak, on an air-cooled cable.

sources.title: ABB E-mobility — Terra 360 UL data sheet (9AKK108468A2521)

facts.claim: The Alpitronic HYC400 (UL) outputs 150–1000 V DC and up to 400 kW with four power stacks, at most 600 A per cable.

sources.title: Alpitronic — HYC400 UL data sheet (V1-2, 2025): DC output and output voltage

facts.note: The 400 kW needs all four power stacks; with fewer, it is 100 kW per stack. The owner remembered it as about 950 V and 600-some A; the data sheet says 1000 V and 600 A. Electrive (Mar 2026) reports the earlier HYC400 at 500 A continuous / 600 A boost, and a Series 2 at 600 A continuous.

facts.claim: DC fast-charging cable ratings vary widely. Liquid-cooled cables are commonly rated 350–500 A continuous. Air-cooled ones are rated 200–500 A continuous, and some boost briefly to 350–600 A.

sources.title: ABB E-mobility — Terra 360 UL data sheet: 350 A nominal, 500 A peak, air-cooled (one consistent example)

facts.rationale: The owner's field experience across many charger models (2026-09-28): a range, not a figure for any one charger. The ABB data sheet is one example inside it. Replaces the earlier claim that '~500 A is common on liquid-cooled CCS1', which the data sheet did not support as written.

facts.claim: Lucid quotes the Gravity's pack at 926 V. EPA's Fuel Economy Guide data lists it at 810 V.

sources.title: Lucid Group press release, 28 Jan 2025
EPA / DOE Fuel Economy Guide data (MY24–MY27 files), total_voltage_v, as imported into EVBench

facts.note: Say 'Lucid quotes 926 V', never 'rated 926 V'. Which point each figure is: see gravity-voltage-points.

facts.claim: Lucid's 926 V for the Gravity is its pack near full charge; the EPA's 810 V is close to its nominal, around half charge.
facts.rationale: The owner's reading (2026-09-28), and it fits the arithmetic: both figures give about 225 cells in series, at about 4.12 V per cell near full and 3.6 V nominal. Neither Lucid nor the EPA says which point it quotes. A product figure, so an explicit owner exception to the accepted rule; context only, nothing rests on it.

facts.claim: The EPA's Fuel Economy Guide data does not file one consistent point on a pack's voltage range: GM's 80-cell Ultium cars appear at 336 V, their full-charge voltage (80 × 4.2 V), while the Gravity appears at 810 V, well below the 926 V Lucid quotes.

sources.title: EPA / DOE Fuel Economy Guide data (MY24–MY27 files), total_voltage_v, as imported into EVBench
Arithmetic against gm-ultium-80s-pack (80 cells: 4.2 V full, 3.6 V nominal) and lucid-gravity-voltage (Lucid's 926 V)

facts.note: The GM half is exact: 336 V is 80 × 4.2 V. The Gravity half shows only that the EPA's figure and Lucid's differ by 116 V; which point each one is rests on gravity-voltage-points (accepted), and this fact does not depend on it. Also recorded in docs/vocabulary.md under 'Why not nominal curve', so EVBench readers of the column see it.

facts.claim: The Gravity charges on 500 V chargers with motor boost: its rear drive unit steps the charger's 500 V up to pack voltage. Lucid contrasts this with pack splitting.

sources.title: Lucid Group press release, 28 Jan 2025

facts.claim: Lucid rates the Gravity at sustained speeds of up to 225 kW on 500 V chargers, including Tesla V3 Superchargers.

sources.title: Lucid Group press release, 28 Jan 2025
Lucid — Public Charging Guide ('up to 225 kW at Tesla Superchargers')

facts.note: EVBench run 81 (Gravity Grand Touring, 'State of Charge (Supercharger)') peaks at 210 kW in the 2026-09-15 dump. Its source field reads 'asdf' and it has no source URL — fix the record before the page links it.

facts.claim: The Gravity charges at up to 400 kW on 1000 V chargers.

sources.title: Lucid Group press release, 28 Jan 2025

facts.claim: Lucid quotes the Gravity's pack at 926 V, above an ABB Terra 360's 920 V maximum output, and a pack's voltage rises further while it takes charge.

sources.title: Arithmetic on two verified facts: lucid-gravity-voltage and abb-terra360-ratings

facts.claim: Lucid vehicles can struggle on some chargers rated 920–950 V, because a hot pack taking charge can meet or exceed that voltage.
facts.rationale: The owner's field observation of Lucid vehicles on chargers rated 920–950 V. An EVBench Lucid charging test on a known 920–950 V charger, showing the limit, would make it rank B.

facts.claim: The Lucid Air boosts on ~400 V Superchargers through its Wunderbox, which limits output to 50 kW.

sources.title: Lucid — Public Charging Guide

facts.claim: The Neue Klasse BMW iX3 can charge from 400 V DC stations, which BMW credits to 'battery management tech with integrated switching matrix'.

sources.title: BMW Group PressClub Global — 'The start of a new era: the new BMW iX3', 5 Sep 2025
BMW Group PressClub USA — 'The All-New BMW iX3'

facts.claim: The iX3 charges on 400 V by splitting its pack into two halves charged in parallel.

sources.title: EVChargingStations.com, 14 Dec 2025 — 'can be split into two 400-volt modules'; cites no BMW document

facts.note: BMW never says 'split' in the three releases fetched; it says 'switching matrix'. Consistent with a split pack (run 121 peaks 194 kW on a V3 Supercharger, which at half of 698.9 V needs ~555 A), but consistent is not confirmed. Page must say 'BMW calls it a switching matrix' until a BMW technical source says more.

facts.claim: The iX3 50 xDrive's pack voltage is 698.9 V.

sources.title: BMW Group PressClub USA — 'The All-New BMW iX3', technical data

facts.claim: The iX3 50 xDrive's usable battery energy.

sources.title: BMW Group PressClub Global, 5 Sep 2025 — 'usable energy content of 108.7 kWh'
BMW Group PressClub USA — technical data, 'Net usable energy content 112.2'

facts.note: Two BMW sources disagree. Read the US technical-data table by hand (it was read through a summariser) before using either figure.

facts.claim: The iX3 charges at up to 400 kW and 10–80 % in 21 minutes on an 800 V charger.

sources.title: BMW Group PressClub Global, 5 Sep 2025

facts.claim: On a Tesla V3 Supercharger, an iX3 50 xDrive peaked at about 194 kW.

sources.title: Bjorn Nyland — 'BMW iX3 50 xDrive charging test on 400 kW, 350 kW and 400 V Tesla' (EVBench run 121)

facts.note: The figure is from EVBench's own run data; the video itself was not watched in this pass. Flip once a curator confirms the run matches the video.

facts.claim: The Mercedes CLA (US) needs a factory-fitted converter to use 400 V DC chargers; it is installed on CLAs from spring 2026. Without it the car charges only on 800 V DC chargers.

sources.title: Mercedes-Benz USA — 2026 CLA Sedan
EV Powered, 28 Nov 2025 — UK: an option (£850) for orders from spring 2026, not retrofittable

facts.note: Verified for the US statement only. Standard-vs-option varies by market; the UK price and 'not retrofittable' are secondary. No source gives the converter's kW.

facts.claim: The CLA charges at up to 320 kW on 800 V DC chargers.

sources.title: Mercedes-Benz USA — 2026 CLA Sedan

facts.claim: The Cybertruck charges on 400 V Superchargers by splitting its pack: a DPDT (double-pole, double-throw) contactor switches its two halves from series to parallel.

sources.title: Smart Charge America — 'E46: The MAGIC behind Tesla's Cybertruck DPDT 400V/800V' (YouTube)
InsideEVs — 'What Is A Split Pack Electric Vehicle Battery?'

facts.note: Supplied by the owner on 2026-09-28 as the definitive source. Claude read the video's title and channel (via oEmbed) but did not watch it. Still no Tesla document (rank A); the InsideEVs piece stays as a secondary source. kW figures are a separate, still-unverified fact (cybertruck-kw-by-charger).

facts.claim: The EPA's Fuel Economy Guide data lists the Cybertruck's pack at 710 V, so each half of its split pack is about 355 V.

sources.title: EPA / DOE Fuel Economy Guide data (MY25–MY26 files), total_voltage_v, as imported into EVBench

facts.note: Which point on the voltage range Tesla filed is not stated (see epa-voltage-points-differ); treat 710 V as a round figure for the class. The owner puts it at about 740 V under charge.

facts.claim: Tesla lists the Cybertruck's Supercharging maximum as 325 kW.

sources.title: Tesla — Cybertruck, specifications ('Supercharging Max/Payment Type: 325kW Max')

facts.claim: Tesla announced 500 kW Supercharging for the Cybertruck in November 2024, and the first full V4 site, opened in October 2025, delivers 500 kW, with the Cybertruck the one Tesla able to use it. At a V4 cabinet's 1000 V it charges as one series pack.

sources.title: @cybertruck (Tesla's official Cybertruck account) on X, 15 Nov 2024: '500kW Supercharging is coming', quoting a @TeslaCharging video (14 Nov 2024) that shows a Cybertruck charging at '500 kW, 1298 mi/hr'

EVWire (Jaan Juurikas), 10 Oct 2025 — 'Tesla officially opens its first fully V4 Supercharger capable of 500 kW car and 1.2 MW truck charging' (Redwood City, CA): 'other Teslas, except Cybertruck, can't use this 500kW … and remain at 250kW'

facts.note: Supplied by the owner (2026-09-28), with a screenshot of the video frame. Tesla's post is an announcement; EVWire (D) reports the site delivering it. 'As one series pack' is arithmetic: at up to 1000 V the charger reaches the whole ~710 V pack (cybertruck-voltage, tesla-v4-cabinet-voltage), so it has no reason to split. Tesla's Cybertruck spec page still lists 325 kW max; it lags the announcement.

facts.claim: At the EPA's 710 V, the Cybertruck's current is about 915 A for 325 kW split (355 V halves), about 700 A for 250 kW split, and about 700 A for 500 kW as one series pack.

sources.title: I = P ÷ V at 355 V (split) and 710 V (series)

facts.note: Derived, not measured: runs record neither pack voltage nor current. Under charge the voltage runs higher than 710 V (the owner puts it near 740 V), so the real currents are a few percent lower: the owner's ~880 A, ~680 A, ~680 A. The ~915 A at 325 kW is above a V4 post's 615 A continuous rating (tesla-v4-post-ratings), so it is a peak, not a steady current.

facts.claim: A battery management system cuts charging power as the cells near their temperature limit, and in fast charging many vehicles hold close to that limit for part of the session. So a lower charging power can hold the car's peak for longer.
facts.rationale: Widely accepted in EV engineering and in EVBench's experience (owner, 2026-09-29): cell heat rises with the square of current (physics-cell-heat-scales-with-current-squared), so power is held against a thermal limit. The Gravity's two charging tests show the effect (gravity-10-80-by-charger).

facts.claim: In EVBench's tests, a Lucid Gravity charged from 10 to 80% in 24.5 minutes at a 418 kW peak on a 1000 V charger, and in 28.6 minutes at a 210 kW peak on a Supercharger: half the peak power, about 17% longer.
facts.rationale: EVBench's own data (runs 23 and 81, 2026-09-15 dump; time at the first point at or above 10% and 80% SoC). Observed rather than rank B because run 81's source reads 'asdf' with no URL; fixing that record makes it rank B.

facts.claim: Tesla enabled the Cybertruck to charge at up to 325 kW on select V4 Supercharger posts in December 2024, and on all V4 posts in North America by 28 January 2025.

sources.title: @TeslaCharging on X, 28 Jan 2025: 'All V4 posts in North America can now charge up to 325kW for Cybertruck'
@TeslaCharging on X, 14 Dec 2024: '@cybertruck can now charge up to 325kW on select V4 Supercharger posts. Rollout in progress.' (from the owner's screenshot)
EVWire, 10 Oct 2025: the first fully V4 site (V4 cabinet) opened then, so the V4 posts of early 2025 were fed by V3 cabinets

facts.note: Verified for what Tesla said: 325 kW on V4 posts. Why a V4 post on a V3 cabinet could do it is v4-post-lifts-v3-cabinet (observed). EVBench run 18 peaks at 317 kW but records no charger.

facts.claim: Hyundai Motor Group's E-GMP charges on 400 V by using the motor and inverter to boost 400 V to 800 V, with no additional components.

sources.title: Hyundai Motor Group — E-GMP unveiling, 2 Dec 2020

facts.claim: The EPA's Fuel Economy Guide data lists the long-range E-GMP cars (Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 6, Kia EV6, Genesis GV60) at 697 V, and the Standard Range EV6 at 523 V.

sources.title: EPA / DOE Fuel Economy Guide data (MY25–MY27 files), total_voltage_v, as imported into EVBench

facts.note: Unlike GM's filings, these read as nominal: 697 V is about 192 cells × 3.63 V, and 523 V about 144 × 3.63 V (cell counts are inference). EVBench's own spec for the IONIQ 5 Base says 523 V, which matches.

facts.claim: Early E-GMP cars reach about 80 kW on 400 V chargers and later ones about 150 kW.
facts.note: From the owner's notes (#355) and already in the max_dc_400v_kw hint. No source found in this pass. See egmp-boost-kw for the owner's current range (120–150 kW, observed); the early-car ~80 kW figure is still unsourced.

facts.claim: Current E-GMP cars (Hyundai Ioniq 5, Kia EV6) boost to around 120–150 kW on a 400 V charger, depending on the model.
facts.rationale: The owner's field experience (2026-09-29), with no hard numbers. EVBench charging tests of an Ioniq 5 or EV6 on a Supercharger (V3) or another 500 V charger, recording the model, would make it rank B and settle which model reaches which figure.

facts.claim: In EVBench's charging tests, a Hyundai Ioniq 5 peaks at about 247 kW and a Kia EV6 GT-Line at about 255 kW.
facts.rationale: EVBench's own data (runs 192 and 238, 2026-09-15 dump), but neither run records its source, so it cannot be cited as rank B yet. Hyundai does not publish a peak kW; secondary press gives 230–260 kW. The owner's rough figure was ~225 kW. Filling the runs' sources would make this rank B.

facts.claim: From the 2025 model year the Taycan has a 150 kW DC/DC converter as standard for 400 V charging; before, it was optional.

sources.title: Porsche Newsroom USA — 'The new 2025 Porsche Taycan models', 6 Feb 2024

facts.claim: The 2025 Taycan charges at up to 320 kW on an 800 V DC charger, 50 kW more than before.

sources.title: Porsche Newsroom USA — 'The new 2025 Porsche Taycan models', 6 Feb 2024

facts.note: EVBench run 45 (Taycan J1.2, the earlier generation) peaks at 313 kW.

facts.claim: The EPA's Fuel Economy Guide data lists the 2025–2026 Porsche Taycan at 850 V.

sources.title: EPA / DOE Fuel Economy Guide data (MY25–MY26 files), total_voltage_v, as imported into EVBench

facts.note: Probably near full charge rather than nominal: 850 V is about 4.3 V per cell if the pack is 198 in series, the plan's unsourced figure. Which point Porsche filed is not stated (epa-voltage-points-differ).

facts.claim: An early Taycan charges at about 50 kW on 400 V chargers.
facts.note: From the owner's notes and the hint. Not researched in this pass (not needed by the two pages).

facts.claim: On a 400 V charger the Audi Q6 e-tron (PPE) divides its 800 V battery into two batteries of equal voltage and charges them in parallel at up to 135 kW; on 800 V it peaks at 270 kW.

sources.title: Audi — 'Focus on charging performance: the new Premium Platform Electric (PPE)', 8 May 2024

facts.claim: GM's Ultium truck platform has 800 V battery packs and 350 kW fast charging; most other Ultium EVs are 400 V, up to 200 kW.

sources.title: GM investor release — 'GM Reveals New Ultium Batteries and a Flexible Global Platform', Mar 2020

facts.note: EVBench runs 48 and 49 (Silverado RST) peak at 346–347 kW, consistent with the truck platform's 350 kW.

facts.claim: The Hummer EV's pack is two 400 V layers in parallel for driving, switched to series (800 V) to fast-charge.

sources.title: Green Car Congress, 22 Oct 2020

facts.note: The plan files GM trucks under 'split pack'. If this is right the framing is inverted: a 400 V pack that series-connects to take 800 V, not an 800 V pack that splits. On a 400 V charger it is in its normal state. Needs a GM technical source. EPA's data lists the 2024 Silverado EV at 290 V and the Hummer EV at 334 V, consistent with packs that drive at ~400 V class and switch to series only to fast-charge.

facts.claim: GM's 85 kWh-class Ultium cars (Equinox EV, Blazer EV FWD and AWD, Optiq, the 2026 Lyriq, Honda Prologue) run 80 cells in series: EPA lists them at 336 V, which is 80 × 4.2 V at full charge, and their nominal is about 288 V (80 × 3.6 V), under 270 V at low SoC.

sources.title: EPA / DOE Fuel Economy Guide data (MY24–MY27 files), total_voltage_v, as imported into EVBench
InsideEVs — 'The 2024 Chevy Equinox EV Tells Us A Lot About Why Voltage Matters' (80S, 288 V nominal, under 270 V at low SoC)

facts.note: Verified by agreement: EPA's 336 V (A) and InsideEVs' 80-series / 288 V (D) are the same pack at 4.2 V and 3.6 V per cell, exactly. No GM document found. The low-SoC figure rests on InsideEVs alone.

facts.claim: GM's smaller-pack Ultium cars charge slowly even on chargers that deliver 500 A.
facts.rationale: The owner's field experience (2026-09-28). It is what the arithmetic predicts for an ~288 V pack (physics-low-voltage-cap); an EVBench Equinox EV charging test on a known 500 A charger would make it rank B.

facts.claim: The EPA's Fuel Economy Guide data lists the Chevrolet Silverado EV anywhere from 290 V to 470 V by year and trim; the 2026 Extended Range is 403 V.

sources.title: EPA / DOE Fuel Economy Guide data (MY24–MY26 files), total_voltage_v, as imported into EVBench

facts.note: 403 V is 96 × 4.2 V, the same full-charge pattern as GM's 80-cell cars (gm-ultium-80s-pack), which fits one of two 96-cell layers at about 346 V nominal. That reading is inference: GM has not said which point, or which configuration, it filed.

facts.claim: Charging split on a lower-voltage charger, a Silverado EV's halves run around 300 V.
facts.rationale: The owner's field experience (2026-09-28). It fits the EPA data read as 96-cell layers (silverado-ev-epa-voltage): about 346 V nominal, lower at the low SoC a fast-charge starts from. An EVBench Silverado test on a Supercharger would make it rank B.

facts.claim: No standard defines the 400 V and 800 V classes. They are industry shorthand: 400 V-class packs sit around 350–450 V nominal, 800 V-class packs around 600 V and above.
facts.rationale: No SAE or IEC document defines the classes (owner, 2026-09-28); makers use the names loosely. BMW sells a 698.9 V pack as 800 V (bmw-ix3-voltage), and Lucid markets 926 V as 900 V+ while EVBench files it as 800 V class. The nominal ranges match the comment on VOLTAGE_CLASS_SPLIT_V in src/utils/platforms.js.

facts.claim: Most EV models in the EPA's Fuel Economy Guide are 400 V class, and the 800 V share is rising: at or above EVBench's 475 V line, 20% of 2024 model entries, 27% of 2025, 28% of 2026, and 36% of the 2027 entries filed so far.

sources.title: EPA / DOE Fuel Economy Guide data (MY24–MY27 files), total_voltage_v, as imported into EVBench
Count of distinct model-year/maker/carline entries with total_voltage_v ≥ 475 V (evbench-voltage-class-split)

facts.note: Entries are the EPA's carline rows, so trims and wheel options count separately. 2027 is partial (129 entries so far); the 2022–2023 files are too thin to use (83 and 32 entries). Makers file different points on the voltage range (epa-voltage-points-differ), which moves few entries across 475 V: GM's full-charge filings stay well below it.

facts.claim: Lower-power and lower-cost EVs mostly use a 400 V-class pack: its power electronics are the more established and cheaper kind, and it charges directly on any DC fast charger.
facts.rationale: Industry common knowledge (owner, 2026-09-29): 400 V was the architecture of the first mass-market EVs, so its components are the most widely made; direct charging follows from the voltage (older-chargers-500v). A supplier or teardown cost comparison would upgrade it.

facts.claim: How an 800 V-class car handles lower-voltage chargers is a trade-off between the pack's voltage and layout, whether its inverter and motor can be designed to convert voltage, and how much cost the maker will accept.
facts.rationale: Engineering judgment, widely shared (owner, 2026-09-29), and visible in the makers' own choices: Lucid argues voltage for motor boost (lucid-gravity-400v-method), Porsche fits a 150 kW converter (taycan-2025-booster), Tesla and Audi split the pack (cybertruck-400v-method, audi-ppe-bank-charging), and Mercedes first shipped the CLA with none (mercedes-cla-400v-method).

facts.claim: EVBench files a vehicle with no electrical platform as 400 V class when its nominal pack voltage is below 475 V, and 800 V class from 475 V up.

sources.title: EVBench's own rule: VOLTAGE_CLASS_SPLIT_V in src/utils/platforms.js

facts.note: A definition, not a claim about the world. The reason for the line (owner, 2026-09-28): it is about the highest nominal voltage that can realistically charge on a charger that tops out at 500 V. The owner confirmed the code's 475 V (2026-09-28). Nearest vehicles in EVBench's specs (2026-09-15 dump): Hyundai IONIQ 6 base at 480 V and IONIQ 5 base at 523 V, both correctly 800 V class. Keep this fact equal to VOLTAGE_CLASS_SPLIT_V.

facts.claim: For its range test, an EV starts fully charged and is driven over repeated cycles on a dynamometer until the battery is depleted and it can no longer follow the cycle.

sources.title: EPA, "Fuel Economy and EV Range Testing" (last updated 1 Jul 2026)
EPA (D. Good), "EPA Test Procedures for Electric Vehicles and Plug-in Hybrids", draft summary, 14 Nov 2017

facts.note: EPA page: "driven continuously over the EPA city cycle until the battery is depleted and the vehicle can drive no further". Good 2017 covers the single-cycle and multi-cycle versions.

facts.claim: The Multi-Cycle Test (SAE J1634, 2012 on) drives city (UDDS), highway and steady-state cycles in one run until the battery is depleted, measuring DC energy out of the battery for the whole test; the car is then recharged from AC with its own charger.

sources.title: EPA (D. Good), "EPA Test Procedures for Electric Vehicles and Plug-in Hybrids", draft summary, 14 Nov 2017

facts.claim: The steady-state (constant-speed) sections of the J1634 Multi-Cycle Test are driven at 65 mph.
facts.note: SAE J1634 is paywalled. EVBench treats 65 mph as specified (SS_CYCLE_SPEED_MPH in src/constants/epa.js). To verify: a public SAE abstract, an EPA or CARB document quoting the MCT schedule, or distance ÷ time on CSI records that report both for an SS phase.

facts.note: Why this is the right basis: the start and end are the same SoC, so the stored energy is equal and the difference is lost, between the port and the pack's DC output (what the inverter draws). That is the span the EPA's DC ÷ AC recharge ratio covers for AC, and the one EVBench's battery-side efficiency is measured on. It includes the cable and port, cooling, heating (the preconditioning on the way in too), auxiliary draw, and the pack's own losses charging and discharging. Precision: the SoC threshold resolves to about 1% of the pack, which on a 25–30 kWh charge is a few percent of error per test; mi/kWh readouts to 0.01–0.1 add the ranges shown. Conditions were not logged (ambient temperature, starting SoC, charger curve), so the spread cannot be assigned to maker or platform: Rivian alone runs 7.7–12.7%, and the two R1Ts, with tight readings, differ by 2.7 points. A 15-minute stop at about 10% SoC may be the high-loss, front-loaded-heating end, so a long 10–80% stop may read lower (a guess, untested); to test that, the owner is looking for 10–80% charges with a same-vehicle range test (70% of range). The Cayenne held 350 kW for much of its session.

facts.claim: EVBench charges the aerodynamic share of a test in proportion to |V_rel|², the square of the air speed, where |V_rel|² = v² + w² − 2vw·cos θ. Averaged over an out-and-back (the angle θ and θ + 180°), the cos term cancels and the cost is v² + w² at any angle: 5000 against 4900 calm, at 0°, 45° and 90° alike (70 mph, 10 mph wind).

facts.claim: With a constant drag coefficient, only the component of the aerodynamic force along the road costs energy: |V_rel|·(v − w·cos θ). An out-and-back then costs 5000, 4975 and 4950 at 0°, 45° and 90° (70 mph, 10 mph wind), so a crosswind costs about half what a head/tail wind does. At 15 mph of wind it is 5125, 5068 and 5011 against 4900 calm.

facts.note: Read from the full paper (the owner's copy, LocalDev/explainers/Reference Docs/). Efficiency = energy taken up by the battery ÷ energy drawn from the grid, per charge event: energy into the battery, not back out of it as EPA counts. Method differs by car: the Volts' FleetCarma loggers read energy received from the EVSE and taken up by the battery (so EVSE losses are left out); the Leafs combined a WattsLeft battery monitor with a Watts Up meter on the EVSE (grid side). Table I gives n = 114 (the abstract says 115). Temperature, from the Results: "high ambient temperatures (> 70°F) reduced charging efficiency of Level 1 charges to 81.4%, but there was no similar effect observed for cold temperatures (< 50°F). Ambient temperature did not appear to affect the efficiency of Level 2 charge events"; too few events below 40 °F to judge. The abstract's "efficiency gains of Level 2 charging also increased under low and high temperatures" is about the gap (Table II: 7.6% below 50 °F, 8.5% above 70 °F, 5.6% overall), which below 50 °F rose because Level 2 read higher, not because Level 1 read lower. from_8kwh_read_by_eye is EVBench's reading of Figure 1 (efficiency against kWh per charge), not a figure the paper states: charges from about 8 kWh up cluster near 86% (83–88) on Level 1 and 88% (86–89) on Level 2, so on full-size charges the gap is about 2–3 points; ±2 points. Several Level 2 events read 97–100%, so single small events are noisy. prior_volt_research is the paper's citation of earlier Volt work (its ref. [2], Hilshey): Level 2 2.7% more efficient on average, 12.8% on events drawing under 2 kWh. Both cars' Level 2 power is not given; the Volt's charger is rated 3.3 kW on 240 V (volt-onboard-charger-inl-2012). ratio_l1_to_l2 is EVBench's arithmetic: 83.8 ÷ 89.4. From Figure 2 by eye: the lowest Level 1 events (about 49%, 60% and 66%) sit between about 31 and 36 °F; two near 72 °F read about 65–66%.

sources.title: A. Kieldsen, A. Thingvad, S. Martinenas, T. M. Sørensen, "Efficiency Test Method for Electric Vehicle Chargers", Proceedings of EVS29, 2016 (peer-reviewed version, DTU Orbit): Table 1, sections 1, 3.4 and 4.3, Fig. 12

facts.note: Read in full from the owner's copy (LocalDev/explainers/Reference Docs/efficiency_paper.pdf). Method 3 (η3, Table 1): discharge the pack 100→80% through the 12 V system with metered energy, recharge 80→100% from metered AC, and subtract the 12 V draw during the charge: η3 = E_discharge ÷ (E_AC − E_12V,charge). So it leaves out the fixed draw, runs a round trip through the DC/DC converter, and covers 80–100% SoC, where the charge tapers to balance cells. Method 1 (η1, iOn only) measures both sides of the charger directly; η3 read 2% below it, which the paper puts down to battery heat, the DC/DC converter (~98%) and inverter standby. CAN-bus readings (η2) were judged unreliable (Leaf spikes above 100%). Battery, section 3.4.1: the iOn's pack voltage rose 2.5 V for a 6.5 A step, "an internal resistance of 0.38 Ω, which is quite small and only result in a heat dissipation of P_loss = I²·R_internal = 7.2 W, when charging with 10 A 230 V". 7.2 W of 2.3 kW is 0.3% (EVBench's arithmetic); the paper squares the 10 A AC current, so the pack-side figure would be smaller. Charger range, sections 1 and 4.4: chargers are tuned to an input range and lose efficiency outside it (Fig. 12, iOn efficiency against AC current); the paper cites a 95% converter losing about 10 points at half power. Three-phase, section 4.3: "A 3-phased charger can use the system voltage of 400 V and use a buck converter to step it down to the MAIN voltage. When only one phase of the charger is used, the line voltage is 230 V and that causes a larger loss in the rectifier and means that a boost converter is needed", the paper's explanation of the Zoe's single-phase result. The Zoe's comparison changes power and phase together. Cars had driven 10–20,000 km; tests were run in a temperature-controlled room.

facts.rationale: Joule heating and Ohm's law (arithmetic), with copper's resistance per length from the standard AWG tables at room temperature (14 AWG ≈ 2.5 Ω and 6 AWG ≈ 0.4 Ω per 1,000 ft). 14 AWG is the smallest copper the NEC allows on a common 15 A outlet circuit. A worked example, not a measurement; the cord gauges are the owner's estimate (2026-11-12) and a lighter one for portable cords: real runs differ in length and gauge, and warm wire resists more. Upgrade with NEC Chapter 9 Table 8.

facts.claim: An onboard charger is often a little less efficient on 120 V than on 240 V at the same power: it draws twice the current, and boosts a lower input voltage up to the pack's. Four of the six cars measured at equal power show it, by 2 to 3 points; two go the other way.
facts.summary: Four of six cars lost 2 to 3 points more on 120 V than on 240 V at the same power.

sources.title: M. Duoba, A. Fernandez Canosa et al., "Development and Evaluation of Distributed Energy Resource Device Models: Electric Vehicles, Electric Water Heaters, and Commercial Refrigeration Systems", NREL/TP-5500-75323 (Argonne, NREL, Oak Ridge), July 2020, Part 1 (Argonne): sections 1.2.2, 1.3.2, 1.5.2.2, Tables 1–4, Figures 15–18
sources.label: Argonne, 2020

sources.title: Idaho National Laboratory, "Steady State Vehicle Charging Fact Sheet" series (INL/EXT-15-34055): 2012 Chevrolet Volt, 2012 and 2015 Nissan Leaf, 2014 BMW i3, 2015 Mercedes B-Class
sources.label: INL steady-state sheets

facts.note: Values are % lost. The Bolt's are from Argonne's loss fits (anl-charging-loss-fits-2020), plug to battery terminals with standby included; the rest are INL's charger-only readings (inl-steady-state-volt-2012, inl-steady-state-leaf-2012, inl-steady-state-leaf-2015, inl-steady-state-i3-2014, inl-steady-state-b-class-2015). The Bolt also lost about ½ point more on 208 V than on 240 V from 3 to 7 kW. Against it: the Volt's 120 V points sit above its 208 V points at about the same power, and the B-Class's efficiency follows current, not voltage, so its 120 V reads higher at equal power; near 1 kW the Bolt's 120 V and 240 V fits agree. Mechanism, from DTU for single-phase 230 V against three-phase 400 V (onboard-charger-loss-dtu-2016): a lower line voltage means more loss in the rectifier and a boost stage up to the pack's voltage; conduction losses also rise with input current, about double on 120 V for the same power. Upgraded from accepted to verified, 2026-11-15, owner's reading of the INL and Argonne data.

facts.claim: Idaho National Laboratory measured a 2012 Chevrolet Volt's onboard charger at 91.7% efficient on 208 V between 3.0 and 3.3 kW, and 90.6% on 120 V near 1.3 kW; with the EVSE included, 90.8% on Level 2 and 88.8% on Level 1.

sources.title: R. B. Carlson, "Advanced Vehicle Testing Activity: Benchmark Testing of the Chevrolet Volt Onboard Charger", Idaho National Laboratory, INL/EXT-12-25761, April 2012

facts.note: Summary: "Charging with Level 2 EVSE at 208 VAC input … 91.7% efficient … Charging with Level 1 EVSE at 120 VAC input … 90.6% efficient while operating near 1.3 AC kW." Efficiency is the charger's combined DC output (high and low voltage) ÷ its AC input, read from the car's CAN data with the key off. The two points differ in both voltage and power, so the 1.1-point gap is not voltage alone. It leaves out the rest of the car's draw while charging (pumps, controllers fed from the pack), so it is not a wall-to-battery figure. The Volt's charger is rated 3.3 kW on 240 V and 1.2 kW on 120 V (its Table 1). Section 3.3: full power is 3.0–3.3 AC kW on Level 2 and 1.2–1.4 AC kW on Level 1, drawn for more than 99% of a typical charge. Not used as an efficiency (owner, 2026-11-15): a steady-state reading of the charger alone, well above the whole-session figures for the same car from Sears et al. (ac-level1-vs-level2-sears-2014) and EPA's certification recharge of the 2011-era Volt (about 80% out of the battery at 240 V), and it misses what a real session spends on top-off, balancing and pack conditioning. Its charging powers (full_power_kw) are still used. INL's 2015 steady-state sheet for a 2012 Volt (inl-steady-state-volt-2012) reads 3 to 4 points lower than this report.

facts.claim: INL found most Level 2 EVSE more than 99% efficient above 3 kW, and a Level 1 EVSE 98% efficient above 1.25 kW.
facts.summary: INL found a Level 2 charging station over 99% efficient, a Level 1 98%.

sources.title: R. B. Carlson, "Advanced Vehicle Testing Activity: Benchmark Testing of the Chevrolet Volt Onboard Charger", Idaho National Laboratory, INL/EXT-12-25761, April 2012
sources.label: INL, 2012

facts.note: From the same report's summary and footnotes: "most Level 2 EVSE are greater than 99% efficient when operating above 3.0 kW (208 to 240 VAC) and Level 1 EVSE are 98% efficient when operating above 1.25 AC kW (120 VAC)". The Level 1 figure is one unit, tested by INL but "not yet published" when the report was written. EVSE efficiency covers the whole unit (its relay, control board and cord), not the cord alone.

facts.claim: Balanced three-phase power puts a third of the current in each of three conductors, so over the same wire it loses about a sixth of what single-phase loses at the same power and phase voltage.
facts.summary: Three-phase wiring loses about a sixth of what single-phase does at the same power.
facts.rationale: Arithmetic from Joule heating: single-phase loss 2·I²R (out and back); balanced three-phase 3·(I/3)²R = I²R/3, with no neutral current. Textbook power engineering, not any one product's figure.

facts.claim: Three-phase home charging is common in Europe, Australia and New Zealand. Three-phase power flows steadily rather than pulsing twice a cycle as single-phase does, which eases an onboard charger's filtering; chargers that take it are built either as three single-phase stages, one per phase, or around a single three-phase rectifier.
facts.summary: Three-phase power flows more smoothly, but many chargers just use three single-phase stages.
facts.rationale: General power-engineering knowledge: balanced three-phase instantaneous power is constant, single-phase power pulses at twice the line frequency, so a single-phase charger needs more energy storage on its DC link. Both charger layouts appear in silicon makers' onboard-charger reference designs. An argument that three-phase is probably a little more efficient, not a measurement; the page says so. Upgrade with a measurement of one car at equal power on one phase and three. DTU gives the input-voltage mechanism for one car, the Renault Zoe (onboard-charger-loss-dtu-2016): three-phase 400 V lets the charger step down to the pack, while single-phase 230 V needs a boost stage and loses more in the rectifier.

facts.claim: The 2013 Chevrolet Volts and Nissan Leafs in the Vermont study charged at about 3.3 kW on Level 2.

sources.title: For the Volt: R. B. Carlson, INL/EXT-12-25761, Table 1 (3.3 kW maximum high-voltage output on 240 VAC; 3.0–3.3 AC kW at full power)

facts.rationale: The owner's knowledge of both cars (2026-11-12): the Volt and the Leaf of that era both charge at 3.3 kW on Level 2. The Volt's figure is sourced (INL); the Leaf's is not, and the Sears et al. paper does not give either. Upgrade with a Nissan specification for the 2013 Leaf's charger fitted to the study cars. Used only to place the study's Level 2 results on the loss-against-time figure.

facts.claim: On EPA certification testing of the 2011 Nissan Leaf, about 87% of the energy drawn from the wall reached the battery, and about 96–97% of what went into the battery came back out, so EPA-basis charging efficiency (out of the battery ÷ from the wall) was about 84–85%.
facts.summary: EPA’s 2011 Leaf test: 87% reached the battery, 84 to 85% came back out.

Pack round trip covers losses inside the pack on charge and discharge plus any drain over the soak, not charge-side loss alone. The city test prints Total DC Energy Output as 73.9, a copy of its regen input; net expended (184.8) implies about 258.7. Only net expended is used here.

facts.summary: EPA’s first-generation Volt test: 80 to 82% of the wall energy came back out.

facts.note: Read from the owner's excerpts of the application, 2026-11-15; the first city test's number was not in the excerpt. The sheet labels the cumulative values Watt-hours, but they are amp-hours: about 4 Ah per 7.47-mile city bag at 350–390 V is about 200 Wh/mi, right for a Volt; read as Wh they make no sense. Bags where the engine runs are included, because the recharge refills all the net charge drawn. Bag 9 of the first city test starts at 30.2 Ah where bag 8 ended at 30.29 (about 0.03 kWh). The 120K tests are of a car aged to 120,000 miles, which fits its smaller total (about 10.3 kWh against 11.1). Each test has one recharge at an unstated current, so it says nothing about how loss changes with charging power. The confirmatory test's date points to model year 2011. Compare INL's steady-state 90.8% for the same car's charger and EVSE (volt-onboard-charger-inl-2012), which EVBench does not use.

facts.claim: In ADAC's 2022 measurements of four electric cars, charging from a household socket at 2.3 kW lost 12.7–24.2% of the energy drawn, an 11 kW wallbox 6.3–9.7%, and a wallbox turned down to 3.5–5.5 kW in between.
facts.summary: ADAC: four 2022 cars lost 13 to 24% on a socket, 6 to 10% on an 11 kW wallbox.

value.unit: % of energy drawn, lost before the battery
value.basis: into the battery (calibrated meter against the battery management system’s stored energy)
value.charge: 20% of the battery added per measurement, same conditions each time

sources.title: ADAC, "Elektroauto und Ladeverluste: So können Sie Kosten vermeiden", W. Rudschies, technical advice L. Kalb (ADAC Technik Zentrum), 2022-09-13; archived copy of the page ADAC has since replaced with its 2026 study
sources.label: ADAC, 2022

facts.note: Method, from the page: each battery was charged by 20% under the same conditions, and the energy from a calibrated meter was compared with the energy stored according to the battery management system. So it is into the battery, like the 2026 round (ac-socket-vs-wallbox-adac-2026), not out of it as EPA counts. The page does not say how many phases the reduced-power charges used: 3.5 kW and 5.5 kW fit three-phase at 5 A and 8 A, and 3.6 kW fits one phase at 16 A, but that is EVBench's inference. The Fiat lost more at 3.6 kW than on the 2.3 kW socket, so its charger does not follow the trend at that setting. ADAC also reports that adding 20% or 50% of the battery made no meaningful difference to the losses. Different cars from the 2026 round; the Zoe's 24.2% and the Fiat's 12.7% equal the 2026 CLA's and Model Y's socket figures by coincidence, which has confused some secondary reports.

facts.claim: Over a year of AC charging, the owner's 2022 Rivian R1T spent about 150 W on its own systems for every hour it charged, plus about 50 Wh per charge; heating the battery took 1.5% of the energy over the year, almost all of it in winter.
facts.summary: The owner’s R1T used about 150 W on its own systems for each hour it charged.

sessions.excluded: 3 flagged corrupted by Roamer, 5 under 1 kWh

thermal.per_charge_note: 28 charges with 1 kWh or more, all near 7 kW: barely related to how long the charge ran (5.3 kWh in 2.1 h on 2026-01-25, 5.2 kWh in 10.4 h on 2026-01-29)

sources.label: EVBench fit

facts.rationale: The owner's own truck, as Rivian reports each charge and Roamer records it; export saved in LocalDev/explainers/Reference Docs/charge_sessions.csv (2026-11-15). The breakdown sums exactly to the energy added, and pack energy over the change in charge gives a median 132.7 kWh, so it is the DC side of the onboard charger: the charger's own conversion loss and the wall-side energy are not in it. So this is the truck's fixed draw downstream of the charger, a floor on its whole fixed draw. Systems energy follows hours spent charging (146 W), not hours plugged in (6 W), so it stops when charging stops. The per-charge 52 Wh is about 20 minutes of that draw, small beside a typical 3-hour top-up's 0.4 kWh. Systems ran higher in summer (181 W) than winter (133 W) while thermal was near zero, so some cooling seems to be booked as systems. Almost every charge was at 7.0–7.4 kW on the home wallbox; the 9.7 and 11.1 kW charges ran 138 and 185 W, but two points cannot show whether the draw changes with power, and there is nothing below 6.4 kW but blips under 1 kWh, so no 120 V comparison. Upgrade with a wall-metered charge of the same truck at 120 V and 240 V.

facts.claim: Fitting each of ADAC's nine cars (2022 and 2026) as a fixed draw plus a share of the power gives fixed draws of 134 to 503 W, median 218 W, and the size of a car's loss at 11 kW barely predicts its fixed draw.
facts.summary: ADAC’s nine cars draw 134 to 503 W while charging, median 218 W.

value.model: loss = P₀ ÷ P + k, through each car’s 2.3 kW socket and 11 kW wallbox results

sources.title: EVBench arithmetic on the per-car tables in ac-socket-vs-wallbox-adac-2022 and ac-socket-vs-wallbox-adac-2026: P₀ = (socket loss − wallbox loss) ÷ (1/2.3 − 1/11) kW, k = wallbox loss − P₀/11
sources.label: EVBench arithmetic

facts.note: Both points are into the battery. The socket is single-phase and the 11 kW wallbox three-phase, so k absorbs any three-phase gain and P₀ any extra single-phase loss. Most of a car's loss at 11 kW is k, which is why it says little about P₀: the ID.3 lost the most at 11 kW (9.0%) and has the smallest fixed draw. Deriving P₀ from the 11 kW figure with a shared k would miss the ID.3 by about 300 W. The fit is two points per car, so it assumes the model's shape; the 2026 cars' 4.1 kW points test it in adac-rate-rule-tested.

facts.claim: Predicting each slower charge from the same car's fast one, with one fixed draw of 200 W for every car, misses ADAC's 2022 and 2026 measurements by 2.0 points on average, against 6.2 for EVBench's old 120 V rule; it does worse than the old rule on the 2013 Vermont cars, whose own fit is about 120 W.
facts.summary: EVBench’s rule misses ADAC’s slower charges by about 2 points on average.

Sears' Level 1 results sit at the Volt's 1.3 kW and Level 2 at 3.3 kW (sears-cars-level2-3-3-kw), which Sears does not state per charge. Leave-one-out: fitting on the other sources and predicting the held-out one.

sources.label: INL, 2013 Leaf

facts.note: Each sheet's "Constant-Speed Range and Charge Testing" table: (C) "Post-test charge AC energy from EVSE @ 240 V to onboard charger", (D) "Post-test charge DC energy into battery from onboard charger", (A+) total DC energy out of the battery including the drives to and from the test (A for the Volt). On-Board Charger Efficiency is D/C, Battery Roundtrip Efficiency A+/D, Overall Trip Efficiency A+/C. The AC is metered at the charging station's output, so the station's own loss (about 1%, evse-efficiency-inl) is left out, and nothing is subtracted for what the car uses while charging, so A+/C is EPA's basis (epa-charger-efficiency-is-ac). Each charge follows a range test, so it runs from nearly empty to full (the Volt's from about 20% to 83.5%, where it switches to the engine). avg_kw is EVBench's arithmetic, C ÷ charge time, so it includes the taper at the end. charge_ambient_c is the sheet's average ambient during the charge. The Focus's 6.6 kW charger is from its specifications; the others' are not given. Battery temperatures during the charges were 24 to 47 °C. The Volt's 70 mph test returned only 88% from its battery after a hot test (no reason given). Both Ford sheets carry the same report number, INL/MIS-15-34211; the Leaf and Volt sheets carry none. One power per car, at 240 V only, so these cannot show how loss changes with power; they show where whole charges of that era landed on EPA's basis. The i3 and B-Class sheets of the series are on avt.inl.gov, which refuses EVBench's machine; not read.

sources.label: INL, 2012 Volt sheet

Steady state means "the RMS current magnitude is not changing and the voltage source is close to nominal", so this is the charger alone at constant current: no fixed draw from the rest of the car, no end-of-charge taper, no charging station loss. Page 2: "As the vehicle charge rate decreases, efficiency decreases … the decrease in efficiency … is not negligible and should be avoided when possible." The equal-power comparison is read from the page 2 chart: near 1.2 to 1.4 kW the 120 V points sit at about 86 to 86.6% and the 208 V points at about 82 to 85%. The same lab's 2012 report on a 2012 Volt (volt-onboard-charger-inl-2012) gave 91.7% on 208 V and 90.6% on 120 V, 3 to 4 points higher than this sheet. facts.claim: Idaho National Laboratory measured a 2014 BMW i3's onboard charger in steady state from 0.66 to 1.33 kW on 120 V, 84.1 to 89.6% efficient, and from 1.38 to 7.22 kW on 240 V, 91.4 to 93.8%; at about the same power, 120 V read about 2 points below 240 V.
facts.summary: The i3’s charger alone: 84 to 90% on 120 V, 91 to 94% on 240 V.

value.basis: charging station output to the high-voltage and 12 V outputs, steady state

sources.title: Idaho National Laboratory, "Steady State Vehicle Charging Fact Sheet: 2014 BMW i3", Advanced Vehicle Testing Activity (footer INL/EXT-15-34055), pp. 1–3

facts.note: Read from the owner's copy, pulled through the Internet Archive because avt.inl.gov refuses EVBench's machine (LocalDev/explainers/Reference Docs/SteadyStateLoadCharacterization2014BMWi3.pdf). Measurement points: "AC Input: EVSE Output", "DC Output: Powertrain Electrical Distribution Module high voltage and 12 volt output"; page 3: "The efficiency in this testing is the efficiency of the on-board charge module." Because the 12 V output counts as output, what the car's systems use while charging is not counted as loss. Key insight, page 1: "The Level 2 efficiency is not strongly influenced by the charge rate." Page 2: "For Level 2 charging, there is a step change in efficiency, power factor and total harmonic distortion at 13 amps or 3 kW." The 120 V maximum is the most a 12 A circuit allows; the 240 V maximum a 32 A circuit. The sheet's footer repeats the Volt sheet's report number. Added at the owner's request, 2026-11-15, as charger-only context. The curve is read from the sheet’s page-2 efficiency chart, which is drawn as vectors: each marker’s center, calibrated to the chart’s own tick marks, with readings within 0.03 kW merged (INL drew two markers per setting and dozens at the top rate). It agrees with the sheet’s table to 0.3 points.

facts.claim: DTU also read what reached the battery from the car's own data, against a meter at the wall: the Nissan Leaf put 85% into its battery at 2.3 kW and 90% at 3.7 kW, the Peugeot iOn 70% and 69%; DTU judged these the least precise of its three methods.

value.basis: into the battery, as the car reports it, against metered AC

sources.label: DTU, 2016

facts.note: Method 2 (η2 = V_D·I_D ÷ P_A): power into the main battery from the car's CAN bus, point D, over AC power from the charging station, point A, averaged over the charge (equation 5). Section 4.1: "the power is decreased when the consumption at point B is increased. This indicates that the EV measures the total flow to and from the MAIN", so the car's own draw while charging counts as loss, as in ADAC's method of comparing a wall meter with the battery management system's stored energy (ac-socket-vs-wallbox-adac-2022). Precision: the Leaf's current is reported in 0.5 A steps, which gave "spikes exceeding 100 % efficiency" before filtering; on the iOn, η2 read 8 to 9 points below the direct measurement (η1), where DTU expected it to read above, which it puts down to "the unknown measure points of the internal measuring network". Both charges ran from 80 to 100% SoC at 19–22 °C (onboard-charger-loss-dtu-2016), so they include the end-of-charge taper.

facts.claim: Argonne metered the AC at the plug and the DC at the battery terminals on a 2017 Chevrolet Bolt, a 2014 BMW i3 and a 2012 Nissan Leaf, counting the car's standby draw as loss, and fitted the loss to the power: at no power the fits start at 151 W for the Bolt on 240 V (177 W on 120 V), 218 W for the i3 and 80 W for the Leaf. At about 1.4 kW the Bolt lost about 2 points more on 120 V than on 240 V, and from 3 to 7 kW about ½ point more on 208 V than on 240 V.
facts.summary: Argonne measured a Bolt, i3 and Leaf, wall to battery, at many charging rates.

facts.note: Read in full from the owner's copy (LocalDev/explainers/Reference Docs/75323.pdf). Section 1.2.2: P_AC is "the total AC power flowing into the charger from the plug", P_DC "the total DC power flowing to the battery", and "The total losses in the onboard charger and from the vehicle standby losses are lumped as a single 'charging loss'"; section 1.3.2: "All standby idle power consumed (not going to the battery) is accounted for in the 'charger' losses model". So it is into the battery, with the car's own draw while charging counted as loss, ADAC's basis. Section 1.5.2.2: "Only steady-state power tests were analyzed"; the spread is "likely from temperature and SoC effects" (neither is stated). Only the Bolt was tested at 120 V and 240 V; the i3 and Leaf at 208 V only. tested_kw is read from Figures 15–17. loss_pct_from_fits and rule_check are EVBench's arithmetic on the fits, inside each tested range. The 120 V fit is loose (R² 0.81) and its points spread from about 180 to 270 W at 1.4 kW in Figure 16; near 1 kW the 120 V and 240 V fits agree, so the voltage gap shows only near the top of 120 V's range. β0 is where each fit meets zero power: a fixed draw plus whatever the charger loses at no load. rule_check runs EVBench's rule (evbench-charging-loss-by-rate, 200 W) from each car's fastest point: it lands within a point on the i3, and overshoots the Bolt by about 4 points and the Leaf by about 6. Section 1.5.2.2 notes the ranking "follows the vehicles age", the newest losing least.

facts.claim: Idaho National Laboratory measured a 2012 Nissan Leaf's onboard charger in steady state from 0.69 to 1.38 kW on 120 V, 84.5 to 86.4% efficient, and from 1.21 to 3.71 kW on 208 V, 88.6 to 88.7%; the charge rate made little difference, and at about the same power 208 V read about 2 points above 120 V.
facts.summary: The 2012 Leaf’s charger alone: 85 to 86% on 120 V, 89% on 208 V.

facts.note: Read from the owner's copy (LocalDev/explainers/Reference Docs/SteadyStateLoadCharacterization2012Leaf.pdf); avt.inl.gov refuses EVBench's machine. Measurement points: "AC Input: EVSE Output", "DC Output: On Board Charge Module Output", the Volt sheet's points. "Vehicle charging is considered to be in steady state when the RMS current magnitude is not changing and the voltage source is close to nominal." Page 3: "The efficiency in this testing is the efficiency of the on-board charge module." Key insight, page 1: "Nissan Leaf Charging efficiency and power quality are not strongly influenced by the charge rate." Page 2's chart: the 208 V points run about 88.6 to 89.6%, peaking near 2 kW; the 120 V points about 84.5 to 86.5%. The equal-power comparison is the table's 120 V maximum (1.38 kW) against its 208 V minimum (1.21 kW). The 3.3 kW charger's 208 V maximum is 3.71 kW. The curve is read from the sheet’s page-2 efficiency chart, which is drawn as vectors: each marker’s center, calibrated to the chart’s own tick marks, with readings within 0.03 kW merged (INL drew two markers per setting and dozens at the top rate). It agrees with the sheet’s table to 0.3 points.

facts.note: Read from the owner's copy (LocalDev/explainers/Reference Docs/fact2014bmwi3ev.pdf and fact2015mercedesbclass.pdf); avt.inl.gov refuses EVBench's machine. Same method as inl-baseline-recharge-2013: (C) "Post-test charge AC energy from EVSE @ 240 V to onboard charger", (D) "Post-test charge DC energy into battery from onboard charger", (A+) total DC energy out of the battery; charger_eff = D/C, round_trip = A+/D, overall_eff = A+/C. The i3's 70 mph charge: note 16, "The battery roundtrip efficiency being greater than 100% is a result of the BMS allowing less energy to be input in the subsequent charge event than it allowed to output during the range test", so its 82% charger figure is low for the same reason. B-Class, note 11: "Vehicle was charged with an EVSE current setting of 16 A (AC) due to facility limitations", about 3.8 kW against its 10 kW charger; its 45 mph D was not recorded (N/A), so overall_eff there is from the sheet. Range Plus widens the battery's operating window ("using RANGE PLUS shortens the service life of the battery"). Battery temperature was not collected for either car.

facts.claim: Car and Driver's long-term 2019 Tesla Model 3 Long Range Dual Motor averaged 95% charging efficiency on a Tesla 240 V wall connector; staff charging on 120 V outlets saw at best 85%, and as little as 60% in very cold weather.
facts.summary: Car and Driver’s Model 3: 95% on 240 V, at best 85% on 120 V.

sources.label: Car and Driver, 2021

facts.note: Read in the built-in browser (the fetch tool got a 403). Quote: "Our long-term 2019 Tesla Model 3 Long Range Dual Motor test car is currently averaging 95 percent efficiency from a Level 2 Tesla 240-volt wall connector. Staffers charging at home using a typical 120-volt wall outlet saw efficiency from, at best, 85 percent, and it dropped to as little as 60 percent in very cold weather, when charging the battery requires expending significant energy to keep it warm." Rank D by the owner's choice, 2026-11-15: the method, charging current and number of charges are not stated, and the 120 V figures are staff's own home charges. It reads as into the battery (likely the car's reported energy added against a meter), ADAC's basis: the same article gives 99% at a Supercharger, which only a meter downstream of the DC conversion would show. The 2019 Long Range's onboard charger is not stated in the article. Owner's reading: the about 10-point drop from Level 2 to 120 V fits the rule; from 95% at the car's top rate the rule gives about 83% at 1.44 kW, 1 to 2 points below the staff's best. The cold low is battery warming, which EVBench prices separately (evbench-battery-warming). The article also cites the 2021 Model Y Long Range's EPA certification, 87.868 kWh from the wall for 77.702 kWh ("a 13 percent overage"), on EPA's basis.
